# General bacteriology

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Basics of infectious diseases > General bacteriology*

[Original Article Link](/library/In0Yug)

---

## Summary

Bacteria constitute a domain of unicellular <u>prokaryotes</u> that, unlike the <u>eukaryotic</u> domain (e.g., animals and plants), do not have a <u>nucleus</u>. They can be classified as pathogens or <u>commensals</u>. Microscopy (with staining) and culture are the most important methods of identifying bacteria. For a table of the bacteria with the highest clinical relevance see “<u>Bacteria overview</u>.”

---

## Occurrence in humans

### Commensals of the human body [[1]](/library/v8aAom)[[2]](/library/ASYRXK)




<u>Commensals</u> are microorganisms (e.g., bacteria, fungi) living on or within humans that do not harm the host under normal circumstances and may even be beneficial (e.g., by inhibiting the growth of pathogens or helping with digestion)




* Resident flora: microorganisms that are permanently present

* Normal skin flora: <u>Staphylococcus epidermidis</u>

* Normal nasal flora: <u>Staphylococcus epidermidis</u>

* Normal oropharyngeal flora: <u>Viridans group streptococci</u>

* Normal flora of <u>dental plaques</u>: <u>Streptococcus mutans</u>

* Normal gut flora: <u>Escherichia coli</u> and <u>Bacteroides</u>

* Normal vaginal flora: <u>Lactobacillus acidophilus</u> (maintain <u>pH</u>)

* Normal lung flora: <u>Neisseria</u> catarrhalis, <u>alpha-hemolytic</u> <u>streptococci</u>, <u>staphylococci</u>, nonpathogenic <u>corynebacteria</u>, <u>Candida albicans</u>

* Transient flora: microorganisms that are temporarily present (e.g., <u>E. coli</u> or <u>S. aureus</u> on hands)





### Pathogens [[1]](/library/v8aAom)[[2]](/library/ASYRXK)




Among the vast variety of bacteria, only very few are considered pathogenic and cause disease in humans. These can be differentiated into:




* Facultative pathogens

* Are capable of survival outside of a host (e.g., in water or soil): e.g., <u>E. coli</u>, <u>Vibrio cholerae</u>, <u>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</u>

* Only cause disease in susceptible hosts

* Opportunistic pathogens

* Usually benign but have the ability to cause disease in an <u>immunocompromised</u> host (e.g., patients with <u>AIDS</u>, patients that undergo <u>chemotherapy</u>)

* Examples of opportunistic infections include:

* <u>Oral candidiasis</u>, <u>vaginal yeast infection</u>

* <u>Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia</u>

* <u>Cytomegalovirus infection</u>

* <u>Cryptococcal meningitis</u>, <u>toxoplasma encephalitis</u>

* Obligate pathogens

* Can only replicate inside the cells of a host and therefore must infect someone in order to survive: e.g., <u>Salmonella</u>, <u>Treponema pallidum</u>, <u>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</u>

* If a sufficient amount of bacteria is ingested (e.g., oral or contaminated foods), disease also occurs in immunocompetent individuals.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Immunocompromise</u> (e.g., due to <u>AIDS</u>, organ transplant), disruption of <u>resident flora</u> balance (e.g., due to <u>antibiotics</u>), or spread of <u>resident flora</u> to otherwise sterile areas (e.g., gastrointestinal <u>E.coli</u> entering the <u>urethra</u>) can facilitate the excessive multiplication and/or spread of organisms, causing infection.

See “<u>Prokaryotes vs. eukaryotes</u>.”

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Cytoplasmic membrane | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Bilayer of phospholipids: contains <u>proteins</u> (e.g., <u>penicillin-binding proteins</u>) and enzymes<br><br> | <br><br>* Hydrophobic layer with selective permeability<br><br>* Contains metabolic enzymes for:<br><br>* Transport<br><br>* <u>DNA replication</u><br><br>* Oxidative metabolism<br><br>* <u>Peptidoglycan</u> cross-linking<br><br>* <u>Penicillin-binding proteins</u> (<u>PBP</u>): <u>cell wall</u> synthesis<br><br><br> |
| Bacterial capsule | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br><br>* Organized layer of <u>polysaccharides</u><br><br>* Highly charged, <u>hydrophilic</u><br><br>* Rarely contains <u>proteins</u><br><br>* <u>Bacillus anthracis</u> contains <u>poly-D-glutamate</u><br><br><br> | <br>* A major <u>virulence factor</u> that protects against <u>phagocytosis</u> and <u>complement</u>-mediated lysis<br><br> |
| <u>Glycocalyx</u> (slime layer) | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Loose <u>polysaccharide</u> net<br><br> | <br>* Adhesion of bacteria to cell surface and foreign surface (e.g., <u>central lines</u>)<br><br> |
| Periplasm | <br>* Absent<br><br> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br><br>* Space between the <u>outer membrane</u> and the <u>cytoplasmic membrane</u><br><br>* Contains <u>peptidoglycan</u> and <u>beta-lactamase</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Stores substances for excretion/elimination<br><br> |
| <u>Flagellum</u> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* <u>Proteins</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Adhesion<br><br>* Motility<br><br><br> |
| Pilus (<u>fimbria</u>) | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Present<br><br> | <br>* Glycoproteins<br><br> | <br><br>* Adhesion of bacteria to cell surface<br><br>* Function as sex pilus (an appendage encoded for the <u>F factor</u> that attaches two bacterial cells together) during conjugation<br><br><br> |
| Endospores | <br>* Present (only <u>gram‑positive</u> bacteria are <u>spore formers</u> )<br><br> | <br>* Absent<br><br> | <br><br>* Coating layer composed of<br><br>* <u>Keratin</u><br><br>* Dipicolinic acid (in the core)<br><br>* <u>Peptidoglycan</u><br><br>* <u>DNA</u><br><br>* Metabolically inactive (spores are usually formed when <u>nutrients</u> are reduced)<br><br><br> | <br>* Aids in bacterial survival by protecting against:<br><br>* <u>Dehydration</u><br><br>* Temperature damage (can only be killed by <u>autoclaving</u>)<br><br>* Chemical damage<br><br> |

## Distinguishing characteristics

### Form




* <u>Bacilli</u>: rod-shaped bacteria

* Cocci: sphere-shaped bacteria that tend to have different arrangements under the microscope and are classified accordingly

* <u>Staphylococci</u> (cluster of <u>cocci</u>): grape-like <u>clusters</u>

* <u>Streptococci</u> (chain of <u>cocci</u>): usually arranged in chains

* <u>Diplococci</u>: usually arranged in pairs

* Coccobacilli: very short rods almost resembling <u>cocci</u>

* <u>Spirochetes</u>  

* Spiral-shaped organisms

* Contain axial filaments (endoflagella)

* Poorly visible on <u>Gram stain</u>

* Include: <u>Treponema pallidum</u>, <u>Borrelia burgdorferi</u>, and <u>Leptospira interrogans</u>

* Usually diagnosed by dark-field microscopy;  (a microscopy technique that illuminates specimens against a dark background) and <u>serologic studies</u>

### <u>Cell wall</u> structure




#### Gram staining




* Description: a standard microbiological <u>laboratory method</u> used to differentiate bacteria based on their <u>cell wall</u> structure

* Method
1. * Application of <u>crystal violet</u> to a previously heat-fixed smear of a <u>bacterial culture</u>
2. * Addition of <u>iodine</u> to trap the dye
3. * Washing out of dye with acetone or ethanol
4. * <u>Counterstain</u> with safranin (or in some cases carbol fuchsin)

* Results  

* Gram-positive bacteria have a thick <u>peptidoglycan</u> <u>cell wall</u> that traps <u>crystal violet</u> → violet-to-blue appearance

* Gram-negative bacteria have a thin <u>peptidoglycan</u> <u>cell wall</u> that does not trap <u>crystal violet</u> but does retain the <u>counterstain</u> (e.g., safranin) → pink appearance
* Atypical bacteria are bacteria that do not <u>Gram stain</u> well (remain colorless and are therefore often considered <u>gram negative</u>). Reasons include:

* Lack of <u>cell wall</u> (e.g., <u>Mycoplasma</u>, <u>Ureaplasma</u>)

* <u>Atypical cell</u> wall composition (e.g., high lipid percentage in <u>Mycobacteria</u>, lack of <u>peptidoglycan</u> in <u>Chlamydia</u>, lack of <u>lipopolysaccharide</u> in <u>Treponema</u>)

* Very thin <u>cell wall</u> (e.g., <u>Leptospira</u>)

* Bacteria are intracellular (e.g., <u>Chlamydia</u>, <u>Legionella</u>, <u>Rickettsia</u>, <u>Bartonella</u>, <u>Ehrlichia</u>, <u>Anaplasma</u>)





![Cell walls of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria](media/xp1hj81aomf115kb3o7jk2i5.jpg)

Cell walls of gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria

![Overview of bacteria](media/svpfgz9gdmuhz5qfdw1di9jh.jpg)

Overview of bacteria




#### Acid-fast staining




* Description: a method that stains mycolic acid, which is contained in <u>the cell</u> wall of acid-fast bacteria (e.g., <u>Mycobacteria</u>, <u>Nocardia</u>).

* <u>Ziehl-Neelsen stain</u>: produces red staining

* <u>Auramine-rhodamine stain</u>

* Yellowish-red staining

* More commonly used for screening due to higher <u>sensitivity</u> and lower cost compared to <u>Ziehl-Neelsen staining</u>





> [!NOTE]
> “These Atypical Microbes Usually Lack Color Because these Microbes are Bare (no <u>cell wall</u>), Emaciated (thin), and Remain inside:” Treponema, Anaplasma, Mycobacteria, Ureaplasma, Leptospira, Chlamydia, Borrelia, Mycoplasma, Bartonella, Ehrlichia, and Rickettsia do not <u>Gram stain</u> well.




### Capsule




* Description: a <u>polysaccharide</u> structure located outside <u>the cell</u> membranes of certain bacteria

* Function

* Antiphagocytic by impeding <u>opsonization</u>

* Facilitates adherance to surfaces

* Provides protection from <u>free radicals</u> and heavy metal irons

* Most important encapsulated bacteria

* Group B <u>streptococcus</u>

* <u>Streptococcus pneumoniae</u>

* <u>Haemophilus influenzae type b</u>

* <u>Neisseria meningitidis</u>

* <u>E. coli</u>

* <u>Salmonella</u>

* <u>Klebsiella pneumoniae</u>

* <u>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</u>

* Clinical relevance

* Important <u>virulence factor</u>

* Target of <u>immunization</u>: <u>vaccines</u> against <u>encapsulated bacteria</u> usually consist of a capsular <u>polysaccharide</u> and a protein conjugate (serves as an <u>antigen</u>). See “<u>Management of asplenic patients</u>.”





### Intracellular bacteria




* <u>Obligate intracellular bacteria</u>

* Cannot produce <u>ATP</u> outside of their host cell

* Examples include <u>Rickettsia</u>, <u>Chlamydia</u>, Coxiella

* See “<u>Obligate intracellular bacteria</u>” in “<u>Bacteria overview</u>.”

* Facultative intracellular bacteria

* Can produce <u>ATP</u> outside of their host cell

* Examples include <u>Mycobacterium</u>, <u>Salmonella</u>, <u>Neisseria</u>, <u>Listeria</u>, Francisella, <u>Legionella</u>, <u>Yersinia</u>, <u>Brucella</u>





### Survival in oxygenated environment




Oxygen level is used to differentiate between the following:




* Microaerophile bacteria: grow under subatmospheric oxygen levels (e.g., <u>Helicobacter pylori</u>)

* Anaerobic bacteria

* Obligate anaerobe: grows only in the absence of oxygen (e.g., <u>Clostridium</u>, <u>Actinomyces israelii</u>, <u>Bacteroides</u>, <u>Fusobacterium</u>)

* Occur in the gut flora (pathogenic in other places)

* Susceptible to oxidative damage due to lack of enzymes that can detoxify oxygen radicals (e.g., <u>catalase</u>, <u>superoxide dismutase</u>

* Often produce a foul <u>smell</u> (due to <u>short-chain fatty acids</u>) and gases (CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>) in tissue

* Difficult to culture

* Facultative anaerobe: can use oxygen for <u>ATP generation</u> but may switch to <u>anaerobic metabolism</u> (e.g., fermentation) when necessary (e.g., <u>Staphylococcus</u>, <u>Streptococcus</u>, and <u>gram‑negative</u> bacteria in the gut)

* Aerobic bacteria

* Require oxygen to produce <u>ATP</u>

* Grow optimally under atmospheric oxygen levels

* Examples include <u>P. aeruginosa</u>, <u>M. tuberculosis</u>, <u>B. pertussis</u>, <u>Nocardia</u>





> [!NOTE]
> “Foul Anaerobes Can't Breathe:” Fusobacterium, Actinomyces israelii, Clostridium, and Bacteroides are obligate anaerobic.




### <u>Hemolysis</u>




<u>Hemolysis</u> serves to differentiate <u>streptococci</u> based on the various types of <u>hemoglobin</u> degradation




* Alpha hemolysis

* <u>Hemoglobin</u> present in the agar is partially oxidized → <u>methemoglobin</u>, a substance with a characteristic <u>biliverdin</u>-green color (green hemolysis).

* Characteristic of <u>gram‑positive</u> <u>cocci</u> (e.g., <u>S. pneumoniae</u>, <u>viridans streptococci</u>)

* Beta hemolysis

* Complete degradation of <u>hemoglobin</u> with a translucent halo around the bacterial colony.

* Characteristic of <u>gram‑positive</u> <u>cocci</u> (e.g., <u>S. aureus</u>, <u>S. pyogenes</u>, <u>S. agalactiae</u>)

* Lancefield groups: further classify <u>β-hemolytic</u> <u>streptococci</u> according to the specific <u>bacterial cell wall</u> <u>carbohydrate</u> composition

* Gamma hemolysis: no induction of <u>hemolysis</u> (agar around colonies remains unchanged)

* Other: Growth on bile-esculin agar as well as 6.5% NaCl is only exhibited by group D <u>streptococci</u> (<u>enterococci</u>).





![Types of hemolysis](media/kd8zrycbpnnp4j1vuzhhu39r.jpg)

Types of hemolysis




### Enzymatic testing



* Indole test: diagnostic test to differentiate between different members of the <u>Enterobacteriaceae</u> family

* Indole-positive: can convert <u>tryptophan</u> to indole → test medium turns pink (e.g., <u>E. coli</u>)

* Indole-negative: cannot convert <u>tryptophan</u> to indole → test medium remains yellow (e.g., <u>Klebsiella</u> spp., <u>Enterobacter</u> spp.)




### Antibiotic resistance testing




* Antibiotic sensitivity testing: assesses the susceptibility of a bacterial <u>pathogen</u> to various <u>antibiotics</u>.

* Reports the <u>sensitivity</u> of a <u>pathogen</u> as "susceptible", "intermediate", or "resistant" (e.g., <u>Enterococci</u> are resistant to <u>cephalosporins</u>)

* Minimum inhibitory concentration: the lowest concentration of an antimicrobial that inhibits the growth of a specific microorganism isolate

* Can be used to tailor <u>antibiotic therapy</u>

* Antibiogram [[3]](/library/l9Wvnn0)

* Collates the results of <u>antibiotic sensitivity tests</u> in a hospital or region to predict the potential local susceptibility of a bacterial <u>pathogen</u> to various <u>antibiotics</u>

* Typically presented as a table

* Used to determine choice of <u>empiric antibiotic</u> while awaiting <u>antibiotic sensitivity tests</u> for an individual patient





### <u>Growth in culture</u> (bacterial culture)




* Description

* To multiply bacteria for a microbial assay, a tissue or fluid sample is taken from the patient and cultivated on a culture medium.

* Generation time refers to the time required by bacteria to double in number in a culture medium; depends on:

* Species of bacterium (e.g., 20 minutes for <u>E. coli</u> and 12–18 hours for <u>M. tuberculosis</u>)

* Type of culture medium (e.g., the <u>generation time</u> is shorter in specially enriched media)

* The different properties observed in culture allow for the identification of different types of bacteria. 

* Substances in the media (e.g., blood components for the growth of <u>Haemophilus influenzae</u>)

* Surrounding temperature (e.g., cold enrichment for <u>Yersinia</u>

* Types of culture media

* Enrichment culture media: provides optimal conditions for general bacterial growth

* Selective culture media

* Used to grow only select bacteria and thus to isolate specific pathogens

* Contain substances (e.g., <u>antibiotics</u>) that prevent the growth of other organisms

* Example: <u>Thayer-Martin agar</u>

* Indicator media (differential media)

* Contain indicator substances that undergo a change in color when coming in contact with metabolic products of certain organisms

* Example: <u>MacConkey agar</u>

| Triple sugar iron agar | <br>* Contains the fermentable sugars <u>lactose</u>, <u>sucrose</u>, <u>glucose</u>, as well as <u>iron</u> and further <u>nutrients</u><br><br> | <br>* Fermentation causes a color change within the medium<br><br> |  |
| Mannitol salt agar | <br>* High level of salt inhibits the growth of most other bacteria<br><br> | <br>* <u>Gram-positive bacteria</u>, specifically <u>Staphylococcus</u> species<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>S. aureus</u>: golden yellow colonies<br><br>* Other <u>Staphylococcus</u> spp.: no color change in the medium<br><br><br> |
| Bile esculin agar | <br>* Contains <u>bile</u>, esculin, and ferric <u>citrate</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>S. gallolyticus</u>, <u>Enterococcus</u> species<br><br> | <br>* Blackening of the medium around the colonies<br><br> |
| Thiosulfate citrate bile salts sucrose agar | <br>* Contains <u>sodium thiosulfate</u>, <u>sodium</u> <u>citrate</u>, <u>sodium</u> <u>chloride</u>, saccharose, proteose peptone, and further <u>nutrients</u><br><br> | <br>* Vibrio species, <u>Enterococcus</u> species<br><br> | <br>* Round, smooth, glistening, and slightly flattened yellow colonies<br><br> |





### Enzymes




Some bacteria produce enzymes or compounds that aid in survival under certain conditions or allow for <u>colonization</u> of specific organ systems.




* Catalase: an enzyme that visibly breaks down <u>hydrogen peroxide</u> into water and oxygen  , preventing its breakdown into microbiocidal substances (e.g., <u>ROS</u>) via <u>myeloperoxidase</u>  

* Catalase-positive organisms include: <u>Staphylococci</u>, <u>E. coli</u>, <u>Nocardia</u>, <u>Serratia</u>, <u>Listeria</u>, <u>Pseudomonas</u>, <u>Burkholderia cepacia</u>, <u>H. pylori</u>, <u>Bordetella pertussis</u>, <u>Candida</u>, <u>Aspergillus</u>

* Recurrent infections with <u>catalase-positive</u> organisms are common in individuals with <u>chronic granulomatous disease</u> (due to <u>NADPH oxidase</u> deficiency).

* Coagulase: an enzyme that converts <u>fibrinogen</u> into <u>fibrin</u>

* Oxidase (<u>cytochrome c oxidase</u>): an enzyme that catalyzes the donation of hydrogen atoms to oxygen, forming water or <u>hydrogen peroxide</u>

* Microbes that produce <u>oxidase</u> include <u>Campylobacter</u>, Vibrio, <u>Pseudomonas</u>, <u>Brucella</u>

* The colorless phenylenediamine reagent turns dark blue or purple when oxidized.

* Urease: an enzyme that <u>hydrolyzes</u> <u>urea</u> to <u>ammonia</u> and carbon dioxide, which increases the <u>pH</u>

* Urease-producing organisms: <u>Proteus</u>, <u>H. pylori</u>, <u>Ureaplasma</u>, <u>Nocardia</u>, <u>Klebsiella</u>, <u>S. epidermidis</u>, <u>S. saprophyticus</u>, <u>Cryptococcus</u>

* Infections with <u>urease</u>-positive organisms (especially with <u>Proteus</u>) predispose to <u>struvite stones</u>.

* <u>Urease</u>-producing bacteria can colonize and survive in the <u>urinary system</u>.

* <u>Penicillin-binding proteins</u> (<u>PBPs</u>): involved in <u>cell wall</u> synthesis





> [!NOTE]
> “SUCH PuNKS!” - S. epidermidis, Ureaplasma, Cryptococcus, H. pylori, Proteus, Nocardia, Klebsiella, and S. Saprophyticus are <u>urease</u>-positive organisms.




> [!NOTE]
> “A CAT Needs PLACESS to Belch its Hairballs:” Nocardia, Pseudomonas, Listeria, Aspergillus, Candida, Escherichia coli, Staphylococci, Serratia, Burkholderia cepacia, and Helicobacter pylori are <u>catalase-positive</u> organisms.




#### Pigments produced by bacteria




| Bacterium | Produces |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Pseudomonas aeruginosa</u> | <br><br>* Green pigment (<u>pyoverdin</u>)<br><br>* Blue pigment (<u>pyocyanin</u>)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Serratia marcescens</u> | <br>* Red pigment<br><br> |
| <u>Actinomyces israelii</u> | <br>* Yellow <u>sulfur granules</u> (bacterial filaments)<br><br> |
| <u>Staphylococcus aureus</u> | <br>* Yellow pigment<br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> To remember that <u>Pseudomonas</u> aeruginosa produces green pigment, think of the color of a(e)rugula.
> To remember that Serratia Marcescens produces red pigment, think: “flaming hot Serloin (sirloin) Marinade.”
> To remember that <u>Actinomyces</u> israelli produces yellow granules, think of “yellow sands of Israel”.
> To remember that <u>Staphylococcus</u> aureus produces a golden-yellow pigment, think of the word “aurum” meaning gold in Latin.




### Molecular biology and <u>serology</u>




* Molecular biological methods are used (e.g., <u>PCR</u>, <u>FISH</u>) for pathogens that are difficult to cultivate.

* Indirect <u>serology</u> methods are usually used in long-term infections. 

* Qualitative <u>antibody</u> detection

* <u>Titer</u> development

* Detection of specific <u>T-cell</u> reactions, e.g., <u>interferon-γ release assay</u>

* <u>Bacterial toxins</u> can be detected in animal experiments.

## Bacterial genetics

### Bacterial <u>DNA</u> structures




* Plasmids: bacterial nonchromosomal <u>DNA</u> fragments that replicate independently from <u>chromosomal</u> replication

* Integrons: bacterial nonchromosomal <u>DNA</u> that cannot replicate independently (these sequences integrate into <u>chromosomal</u> bacterial <u>DNA</u> via <u>integrase</u>)

* Pathogenicity islands: a group of <u>genes</u> associated with <u>virulence factors</u> such as adhesins and toxins (contain transposase and <u>integrase</u> <u>genes</u>)





### Genetic variability of bacteria




The <u>genetic variability of bacteria</u> is attributable to intracellular and intercellular mechanisms. Bacterial replication occurs solely via binary fission (cell division).




#### Intracellular mechanisms




* High mutation rate

* Exchange of larger <u>gene</u> segments between bacteria that have a similar <u>gene</u> sequence via homologous recombination





#### Intercellular mechanisms




* Bacterial transformation  

* Uptake of free segments of naked bacterial <u>DNA</u> (released by bacterial lysis) from the surrounding through <u>the cell</u> membrane (only competent bacteria) → combination of new <u>DNA</u> material with bacterial pre-existing <u>DNA</u> → degradation of unused <u>DNA</u> → expression of new <u>genes</u> → transformation process

* Bacteria that can undergo transformation include:

* <u>Neisseria</u>

* <u>Haemophilus influenzae type b</u>

* <u>Streptococcus</u> <u>pneumonia</u>

* Deoxyribonucleases break down free <u>DNA</u> and prevent transformation.

* Bacterial conjugation: transfer of <u>plasmids</u> (genetic material) by a bridge-like connection between two bacteria 

* Fertility factor (<u>F factor</u>): bacterial <u>plasmid</u> that enables transfer of genetic material between bacteria   

* F<sup>+</sup> bacteria (donors) have the <u>F factor</u>, which contains <u>genes</u> for <u>sex pilus</u> (to attach to recipient cell).

* F<sup>-</sup> (recipients) do not have the <u>F factor</u>

* F<sup>+</sup> bacteria connect with F<sup>-</sup> bacteria via the <u>sex pilus</u> → a single strand of <u>plasmid</u> <u>DNA</u> (no <u>chromosomal</u> <u>DNA</u>) is transferred from the F<sup>+</sup> bacteria to the F<sup>-</sup> bacteria (mating bridge)

* Result: 2 F<sup>+</sup> bacteria

* Conjugation mediated by <u>Hfr cells</u>  

* Hfr cells (high-frequency recombination cells): bacteria with a <u>conjugative plasmid</u> (e.g., <u>F factor</u>) integrated into their <u>chromosomal</u> <u>DNA</u>

* Hfr bacteria connect with F<sup>-</sup> bacteria via the <u>sex pilus</u> → transfer and replication of <u>DNA</u> material on recipient F<sup>-</sup> bacteria (only the leading part of the <u>plasmid</u> and some adjacent <u>genes</u> are transferred) → F<sup>-</sup> bacteria have new <u>genes</u>

* Result: recombinant F<sup>-</sup> cell with new genetic material and HFr bacteria

* Bacterial transduction  

* The process of <u>gene</u> transfer between bacteria via <u>bacteriophages</u>

* Bacteriophages are <u>viruses</u> that only infect bacteria.

* Infection leads to either the production of a new <u>virus</u> with destruction of the bacterium (lytic phage) or integration of <u>phage</u> <u>DNA</u> into the bacterial <u>genome</u> (prophage).

* Integration of <u>phage</u> <u>DNA</u> can result in acquisition of <u>pathogenicity</u> factors.

* Generalized transduction

* Any portion of the bacterial <u>genome</u> is transferred from one bacterium to another.

* <u>Bacteriophage</u> attaches itself to the <u>bacterial cell wall</u> and injects its <u>DNA</u> into the bacterium → cleavage of bacterial <u>DNA</u> and replication of viral <u>DNA</u> → formation of new <u>bacteriophages</u> with <u>phage</u> <u>capsids</u> containing fragments of bacterial <u>DNA</u> (“packaging error”) → lysis of bacterium and release of <u>bacteriophages</u> → <u>bacteriophages</u> infect other bacteria and thus transfer bacterial <u>DNA</u>

* Specialized transduction (via excision)

* A specific portion of the bacterial <u>genome</u> is being transferred to another bacterium (might include new <u>virulence factors</u>)

* <u>Bacteriophage</u> infects bacteria → viral <u>DNA</u> is incorporated into the bacterial <u>DNA</u> at a specific location but remains inactive (<u>prophage</u> stage) → upon activation;   the viral <u>DNA</u> is replicated and, together with flanking bacterial <u>DNA</u>, excised from the bacterial <u>genome</u> → excised <u>DNA</u> is incorporated in new <u>bacteriophage</u> <u>capsids</u> → lysis of bacterium and release of new <u>bacteriophages</u> → <u>bacteriophages</u> infect other bacteria and thus transfer bacterial <u>DNA</u>

* The <u>genes</u> for the following toxins are transferred from one bacterium to another by <u>specialized transduction</u>:

* <u>Erythrogenic toxin</u> (<u>Streptococcus pyogenes</u>)

* <u>Cholera toxin</u> (<u>Vibrio cholerae</u>)

* <u>Diphtheria toxin</u> (<u>Corynebacterium diphtheriae</u>)

* <u>Shiga toxin</u> (<u>Shigella</u> spp.)

* <u>Botulinum toxin</u> (<u>Clostridium botulinum</u>)

* Bacterial transposition: exchange of genetic information via <u>transposons</u> within the <u>genome</u> or between genomes of various bacteria 

* Transposons: bacterial <u>DNA</u> sequences (jumping <u>genes</u>) that cannot replicate independently [[12]](/library/zSYrXK)

* These sequences can change their position within the bacterium (e.g., from one <u>plasmid</u> to another, to the bacterial <u>chromosome</u>, to a <u>bacteriophage</u>).

* They can copy, insert, reinsert, and excise from different locations along the genetic material of <u>plasmid</u> and <u>chromosomal</u> <u>DNA</u>.

* Development of <u>antibiotic</u> resistance by creating <u>plasmids</u> with different genetic sequences for resistance: <u>Enterococcus</u> (<u>VRE</u>) transfers the <u>vanA gene</u>, which provides resistance against <u>vancomycin</u>, to <u>S. aureus</u> (<u>VRSA</u>).





> [!NOTE]
> SHIN: Streptococcus <u>pneumonia</u>, Haemophilus Influenzae, and Neisseria are capable of <u>bacterial transformation</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> “SHe <u>DI</u>ed BECause of a toxin:” SHiga toxin, <u>DI</u>phtheria toxin, Botulinum toxin, Erythrogenic toxin, and Cholera toxin are transferred via <u>bacterial transduction</u>.

## Mechanism of bacterial infection and disease

### General mechanisms




Bacteria use different mechanisms to colonize, invade, and infect the host in order to survive (<u>virulence factors</u>). In some species, these mechanisms can result in disease. Virulence is a measure of the severity of a disease caused by a <u>pathogen</u>. Calculated by dividing the number of individuals who become severely ill or die due to an infection by the total number of individuals who have contracted the disease.




| Overview of the most common <u>virulence factors</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mechanism | Virulence factors | Function |
| Colonization | <br><br>* Lipoteichoic acid (<u>LTA</u>): a <u>cell wall</u> component present in all <u>gram‑positive</u> bacteria that is anchored in the <u>cytoplasmic membrane</u> and acts as an <u>antigen</u>  [[13]](/library/sGbt0v)<br><br>* Functions as <u>ligand</u> of <u>TLR2</u> → ↑ inflammation<br><br>* Bacterial mutants genetically depleted of <u>LTA</u> show decreased <u>virulence</u>.<br><br>* Bacterial adhesins: colonizing factors<br><br>* <u>Pertussis toxin</u><br><br>* Hemagglutinins<br><br>* Biofilm: a heterogeneous aggregation of bacteria that is held together by <u>extracellular polymeric substances</u> (<u>EPS</u>) [[14]](/library/tGbXav)<br><br>* Enables bacterial adherence to foreign material (e.g., <u>S. epidermidis</u>, <u>viridans streptococci</u>, <u>P. aeruginosa</u>, <u>nontypeable H. influenzae</u>)<br><br>* Protects from clearance mechanisms<br><br>* Flagella: filamentous organelles that aid in the movement of bacteria [[15]](/library/_SY5XK)<br><br>* Peritrichous flagella: <u>flagella</u> around the bacterium (e.g., <u>E. coli</u>)<br><br>* Lophotrichous flagella: several <u>flagella</u> at one pole (e.g., <u>Pseudomonas</u>)<br><br>* Polar flagella: one <u>flagellum</u> at one of the bacterial poles (e.g., <u>Vibrio cholerae</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Adhesion to cell surfaces<br><br>* Invasion of host target<br><br><br> |
| Avoiding the <u>immune system</u> | <br><br>* <u>Bacterial capsule</u><br><br>* IgA protease: cleaves <u>mucosal</u> <u>IgA</u> → adherence and <u>colonization</u> of <u>mucous membranes</u><br><br>* <u>Neisseria</u> spp.<br><br>* <u>Haemophilus influenzae</u><br><br>* <u>S. pneumonia</u><br><br>* Protein A<br><br>* Surface protein found in the <u>bacterial cell wall</u> (e.g., <u>S. aureus</u>)<br><br>* Binds to the <u>Fc region</u> mainly of <u>IgG</u> to prevent <u>immunoglobulin</u> binding to <u>complement</u> or host <u>leukocytes</u> → inhibition of <u>phagocytosis</u>, <u>complement</u> fixation, and <u>antibody</u>-dependent killing mechanisms<br><br>* <u>M protein (virulence factor)</u><br><br>* E.g., <u>S. pyogenes</u><br><br>* Prevents <u>opsonization</u> by C3b → inhibits <u>phagocytosis</u> and alternative <u>complement</u> activation<br><br><br> | <br>* Prevent <u>opsonization</u> and <u>phagocytosis</u><br><br> |
| Bacterial nutrition | <br>* Secretion of siderophores<br><br> | <br>* Chelate and import <u>iron</u><br><br> |
| <u>Antigenic</u> variation | <br><br>* <u>Pili</u>: <u>Neisseria gonorrhoeae</u><br><br>* Capsule and <u>flagella</u> expression: <u>Enterobacteriaceae</u><br><br>* <u>Antigenic drift</u>: <u>HIV</u>, <u>influenza</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Modification of surface <u>antigens</u> to avoid immune recognition and destruction<br><br> |
| Intracellular survival | <br><br>* Inhibition of <u>phagosome</u>-<u>lysosome</u> fusion: <u>M. tuberculosis</u><br><br>* Exiting <u>phagosomes</u> before fusion occurs: <u>Listeria monocytogenes</u><br><br>* Invasins: allow for intracellular translocation of bacteria, evading recognition by the <u>immune system</u> (e.g., <u>Yersinia</u> spp.)<br><br><br> | <br>* Evasion of intracellular <u>phagocytic cells</u><br><br> |
| <u>Type III secretion system</u> | <br>* Injectisome<br><br>* <u>Bacterial appendage</u> that connects bacteria and <u>immune cells</u> and delivers <u>bacterial toxins</u> directly into <u>the cell</u><br><br>* Present in <u>E. coli</u>, <u>Salmonella</u> spp., <u>Yersinia</u> spp., <u>P. aeruginosa</u>, <u>Chlamydia</u><br><br> | <br>* Direct <u>inoculation</u> of <u>bacterial toxins</u> into cells<br><br> |
| Inflammatory response | <br><br>* Bacteria-specific <u>antibodies</u><br><br>* <u>Immune complexes</u><br><br>* <u>Peptidoglycan</u> and <u>teichoic acid</u><br><br>* Toxin released when bacteria die<br><br>* <u>Chemotactic</u> for <u>neutrophils</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Cellular mimicry, e.g., group A <u>streptococcus</u> (<u>rheumatic fever</u> may occur as a result of cross‑reactivity to <u>M protein</u>)<br><br>* <u>Delayed hypersensitivity</u> reactions: <u>Chlamydia</u> (e.g., <u>PID</u>)<br><br>* <u>Granuloma</u> formation: <u>M. tuberculosis</u> and <u>M. leprae</u><br><br><br> |





### Bacterial toxins




#### General




<u>Bacterial toxins</u> are likewise <u>virulence factors</u> and play a role in:




* Bacterial invasion

* Cell damage

* Inhibition of cellular processes

* Stimulation of the <u>immune system</u>





| Overview of the most common <u>bacterial toxins</u> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Endotoxin | Exotoxin |
| Bacteria type | <br>* <u>Gram‑negative</u> organisms only<br><br> | <br>* Both, <u>gram‑positive</u> and <u>gram‑negative</u> organisms<br><br> |
| Location of genetic material | <br>* Genetic information of the <u>endotoxin</u> is encoded in the bacterial <u>chromosome</u><br><br> | <br>* Genetic information of the <u>exotoxin</u> is encoded in the <u>plasmid</u> or <u>bacteriophage</u> that is taken up by the bacterium<br><br> |
| Release mechanism | <br><br>* Bacterial lysis (<u>death</u>)<br><br>* Exocytosis<br><br><br> | <br>* Actively secreted by living bacteria<br><br> |
| Biochemical structure | <br>* Lipopolysaccharide (<u>LPS</u>), which consists of: [[16]](/library/EjY8X6)<br><br>* Lipid A<br><br>* Composed of <u>phosphorylated</u> N-acetyl glucosamine dimer with <u>fatty acids</u> attached<br><br>* Toxigenic component<br><br>* O <u>antigen</u><br><br>* Composed of repeating oligosaccharide subunits<br><br>* Immunogenic component<br><br>* Core <u>polysaccharide</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Polypeptides</u> in the <u>cytoplasm</u>, which consist of two components:<br><br>* Component A (active component): usually an enzyme<br><br>* Component B (binding component): binds to cell <u>receptors</u> and facilitates entrance of A component<br><br> |
| Heat tolerance | <br>* Heat-stable (for one hour at 100Â°C)<br><br> | <br><br>* Heat-labile (quick destruction at 60Â°C)<br><br>* Exceptions: some toxins produced by <u>E. coli</u> and <u>staphylococcal enterotoxins</u>, such as <u>SEA</u> and <u>SEB</u><br><br><br> |
| Antigenicity | <br>* Low<br><br> | <br>* High: induces production of <u>antitoxin</u> <u>antibodies</u><br><br> |
| Mechanism of action | <br><br>* Activates <u>macrophages</u> via <u>CD14</u>/TLR4 <u>receptors</u>, which leads to release of:<br><br>* <u>TNF-α</u> → <u>hypotension</u>, <u>fever</u><br><br>* <u>IL-1</u>, <u>IL-6</u> → <u>fever</u><br><br>* Nitric oxide → <u>hypotension</u><br><br>* Damage to <u>endothelium</u> → release of <u>bradykinin</u> → <u>vasodilation</u> → <u>septic shock</u><br><br>* Activation of <u>complement system</u> (<u>C3a</u> and C5), which leads to:<br><br>* <u>Neutrophil</u> <u>chemotaxis</u><br><br>* <u>Histamine</u> release → <u>edema</u>, <u>hypotension</u><br><br>* Activates the <u>coagulation cascade</u> (via <u>tissue factor</u>) → <u>disseminated intravascular coagulation</u> (<u>DIC</u>)<br><br><br> | <br>* Different mechanism for each toxin such as AB toxins, a two-component toxin:<br><br>* B component facilitates binding and uptake (<u>endocytosis</u>) of A component<br><br>* A component an enzyme, most commonly <u>ADP</u> ribosyltransferases<br><br> |
| Common effects | <br><br>* <u>Fever</u>, <u>flu-like</u> symptoms<br><br>* <u>DIC</u><br><br>* <u>Septic shock</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Tissue and cell <u>necrosis</u> (organ damage)<br><br>* <u>Dehydration</u><br><br>* Usually no <u>fever</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Likelihood of causing disease (toxicity) | <br>* Low: > 100 μg required to cause <u>death</u><br><br> | <br>* High: 1 μg can cause <u>death</u><br><br> |
| Toxoid formation | <br>* Forms no toxoid, therefore, no <u>vaccine</u> available<br><br> | <br>* Forms toxoid that can be modified into a <u>toxoid vaccine</u><br><br> |
| Typical diseases | <br><br>* <u>Meningococcemia</u>, <u>Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome</u><br><br>* <u>Necrotizing enterocolitis</u><br><br>* <u>Septic shock</u> due to <u>gram-negative rods</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Botulism</u><br><br>* <u>Tetanus</u><br><br>* <u>Diphtheria</u><br><br>* <u>Cholera</u><br><br>* <u>Gas gangrene</u><br><br>* <u>Food poisoning</u><br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Lipid A</u> of <u>endotoxins</u> activates <u>macrophages</u> (→ <u>fever</u>, <u>hypotension</u>), <u>complement</u> (→ <u>hypotension</u>, <u>edema</u>, <u>neutrophil</u> recruitment), and the <u>coagulation cascade</u> (<u>DIC</u>).




> [!NOTE]
> “<u>LPS</u> is an ENDOTOXIN:” Lipid A, Polysaccharide, Shock, Edema, Nitric oxide, DIC, Outer membrane, TNF-α, O-<u>antigen</u>, eXtremely heat-stable, IL-1/6, and Neutrophil <u>chemotaxis</u> are important features of <u>endotoxins</u>.




![Effects of endotoxins and exotoxins](media/i2h51jobzgsio8jhpw8umpyt.jpg)

Effects of endotoxins and exotoxins

| Streptolysin O | <br>* <u>S. pyogenes</u><br><br> | <br>* Degrades <u>cell membranes</u>, mainly of <u>RBC</u> → <u>beta-hemolysis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Recent <u>S. pyogenes</u> infection (e.g., <u>pharyngitis</u>)<br><br>* <u>Rheumatic fever</u><br><br><br> |

| Enterotoxin B | <br>* Forms pores in <u>enterocyte</u> membranes → leakage of Na<sup>+</sup> and water into the intestinal lumen<br><br> | <br>* <u>Food poisoning</u><br><br> |  |
| Alpha toxin | <br>* <u>C. perfringens</u><br><br> | <br>* Acts as a phospholipase → degrades <u>cell membranes</u> and tissue.<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Gas gangrene</u><br><br>* Double zone of <u>hemolysis</u> seen on blood agar cultures<br><br><br> |
| Diphtheria toxin | <br>* <u>C. diphtheriae</u><br><br> | <br>* Inactivates <u>EF-2</u> → arrested protein <u>translation</u> and synthesis → <u>cell death</u> and <u>necrosis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Diphtheria</u><br><br>* <u>Myocarditis</u><br><br><br> |
| Pseudomonas exotoxin A | <br>* <u>P. aeruginosa</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Ecthyma gangrenosum</u><br><br> |  |
| Shiga toxin | <br><br>* <u>Shigella</u> spp.<br><br>* <u>Enterohemorrhagic E. coli</u> (<u>EHEC</u>)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Removes <u>adenine</u> from <u>rRNA</u> → inactivation of <u>60S ribosome</u> → disruption of <u>protein synthesis</u> → <u>cell death</u> → GI <u>mucosal</u> damage → <u>diarrhea</u><br><br>* Enhanced <u>cytokine</u> release → microthrombi that occlude the <u>arterioles</u> and <u>capillaries</u> → <u>microangiopathic hemolytic anemia</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, and <u>acute kidney injury</u><br><br>* Only <u>Shigella</u> invades host cells<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Shigellosis</u><br><br>* <u>EHEC</u> <u>gastroenteritis</u><br><br>* <u>Reactive arthritis</u><br><br>* <u>HUS</u><br><br><br> |
| Heat-stable toxin | <br>* <u>Enterotoxigenic E. coli</u> (<u>ETEC</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Activation of <u>guanylate cyclase</u> → ↑ <u>cGMP</u> → ↓ NaCl reabsorption → water efflux into the intestinal lumen → <u>secretory diarrhea</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Gastroenteritis</u><br><br> |
| Heat labile toxin | <br><br>* <u>Enterotoxigenic E. coli</u> (<u>ETEC</u>)<br><br>* <u>B. cereus</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Overactivates <u>adenylate cyclase</u> → ↑ <u>cAMP</u> → ↑ secretion of <u>chloride</u> and water efflux into the intestinal lumen → <u>watery diarrhea</u><br><br> |  |
| Cholera toxin | <br>* <u>V. cholerae</u><br><br> | <br>* Permanently activates <u>G<sub>s</sub> protein</u> → overactivation of <u>adenylate cyclase</u> → ↑ <u>cAMP</u> → ↑ secretion of <u>chloride</u> and water efflux into the intestinal lumen → <u>watery diarrhea</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Cholera</u> (rice-water <u>diarrhea</u>)<br><br> |
| Anthrax toxin | <br>* <u>B. anthracis</u><br><br> | <br>* Consists of <br><br>* <u>Edema factor</u> (EF): binds to <u>calcium</u> and <u>calmodulin</u> and gains <u>adenylate cyclase</u> activity → ↑ <u>cAMP</u> → cell <u>edema</u><br><br>* <u>Lethal factor</u> (LF): a metalloprotease that destroys MAPKK → <u>cell death</u><br><br>* Protective <u>antigen</u>: binds to <u>endothelial</u> <u>receptors</u> and facilitates entry of EF and LF into host cells<br><br> | <br>* <u>Cutaneous anthrax</u> (black <u>eschar</u>)<br><br> |
| Pertussis toxin | <br>* <u>B. pertussis</u><br><br> | <br>* Causes <u>ADP-ribosylation</u> of the α subunit of <u>G<sub>i</sub> protein</u> → inhibition of <u>G<sub>i</sub> protein</u> → <u>adenylate cyclase</u> disinhibition → <u>cAMP</u> accumulation → impaired <u>cell signaling</u> pathways<br><br> | <br>* <u>Pertussis</u> (<u>whooping cough</u>)<br><br> |
| Tetanospasmin | <br>* <u>C. tetani</u><br><br> | <br>* Acts as <u>protease</u> that cleaves <u>synaptobrevin</u> (<u>SNARE protein</u>) → prevention of inhibitory <u>neurotransmitters</u> (i.e., <u>GABA</u> and <u>glycine</u>) release from <u>Renshaw cells</u> in the spinal cord → uninhibited activation of <u>alpha motor neurons</u> → muscle spasms, rigidity, and <u>autonomic instability</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Tetany</u><br><br> |
| Botulinum toxin | <br>* <u>C. botulinum</u><br><br> | <br>* Acts as a <u>protease</u> that cleaves <u>SNARE proteins</u> and prevents fusion of transmitter-containing <u>vesicles</u> with the presynaptic membrane → inhibition of <u>acetylcholine</u> release from the presynaptic <u>axon</u> terminals<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Infant botulism</u><br><br>* Food borne <u>botulism</u><br><br><br> |

## Mechanisms of drug resistance

### Genetic mechanisms




* <u>Chromosomal</u>: via <u>chromosomal</u> mutations that alter the binding site for the drug or affect the permeability of the drug

* Extrachromosomal

* Resistance plasmid

* Carries <u>genes</u> for enzymes that create resistance to specific <u>antibiotics</u>

* Consists of:

* Resistance transfer factor (R factor): codes for transfer and replication of resistance <u>genes</u> (can also contain <u>F factor</u>)

* Resistance determinant (r): <u>genes</u> for resistance

* ß-lactamase: an enzyme that breaks the <u>beta-lactam</u> ring of a <u>beta-lactam</u> <u>antibiotic</u>, altering the chemical structure of the drug

* Acetyltransferase: an enzyme that transfers acetyl groups to <u>antibiotics</u>, altering the chemical structure of the drug

* Protein pumps: a group of energy-dependent <u>proteins</u> that pump <u>antibiotics</u> out of <u>the cell</u>





### Nongenetic mechanisms [[17]](/library/pPXLfy)




* Spores

* Loss target structures: such as the binding site of the drug (<u>PBPs</u>), <u>RNA polymerase</u>, <u>ribosomes</u>, and <u>cell wall</u>
